interest against pollution originating outside its boundaries—^is entirely 
unaffected by the development of standing doctrines.” Robert V. Percival, 
Massachusetts v. EPA: Escaping the Common Law's Growing Shadow, 2007 
Su p. Ct . Re v . Ill, 134 (2007). Professors Kathryn Watts and Amy Wildermuth 
agree with Percival, but add a new analytic twist. See Kathryn A. Watts & 
Amy J. Wildermuth, Massachusetts v. EPA: Breaking New Ground on Issues 
Other Than Global Warming, 102 Nw. U. L. Re v . COLLOQUY 1 (June 11, 2007). 
According to them, states have three types of interests, not two: proprietary 
interests, quasi-sovereign interests, and sovereign interests. This last interest 
arises from the fact that the federal regulatory scheme directly or indirectly 
limits the state’s authority to govern its own affairs within its own borders. 
Watts and Wildermuth contend that states—Shaving given up some of their 
authority to the federal government—have a Tenth Amendment interest in 
securing observance of the terms under which they participate in the federal 
system. Imphcit in those terms is the idea that when the federal government 
takes responsibility for the health and welfare of a state’s citizens through 
federal regulation, it will carry out the regulatory program as adopted. And, 
the authors note, Massachusetts v. EPA was decided against the backdrop of a 
very pubhc dispute between California and the EPA over whether California 
should be allowed to set its own motor vehicle emissions standards to regulate 
greenhouse gases.
To the extent that states have special standing to pursue remedies for 
regulatory inaction on the part of the federal government, this status enhances 
the role of state attorneys general in pubhc interest htigation. In some sense, 
this seems perfectly appropriate. State attorneys general are generahy elected 
officials and are expected to represent the pubhc interest of their respective 
states. They might, therefore, be considered to be in a stronger position to 
assert that a “pubhc action”—that is, an action to protect the pubhc interest— 
is safer in their hands than in the hands of a private party or organization that 
is a “self-appointed” defender of the pubhc. Private parties bringing pubhc 
actions should, therefore, appropriately be required to show that they or their 
members are among the injured. The representativeness of an elected official 
is more easily presumed. See, e.g., Bradford Mank, Should States Have Greater 
Standing Rights Than Ordinary Citizens'?: Massachusetts v. EPA’s New 
Standing Test for States, 49 Wm. & MARY L. Re v . 1701 (2008).
A number of recent cases have dealt with standing by states, though they 
do not necessarily touch on the Massachusetts v. EPA formulation or provide 
revealing insight into what “special sohcitude” might imply. If nothing else, 
however, they tend to show that “special sohcitude” does not exempt states 
from standard standing analysis.
